_about: answer = index of the right option (shuffled on screen); evidence = supporting sentence, review only; hint = gentle "look again" line.

glass-house.q: How did Alice get into the Looking-glass room?
options: She went through the glass over the mantelpiece
glass-house.evidence: In another moment Alice was through the glass, and had jumped lightly down into the Looking-glass room.
glass-house.hint: Look again at the part where the glass begins to melt away.

glass-house.q: Why could Alice only read the poem by holding it up to a glass?
options: It was a Looking-glass book, so the words went the wrong way
It was written in a secret code
glass-house.evidence: And if I hold it up to a glass, the words will all go the right way again.”
glass-house.hint: Look again at the part where Alice finds the book on the table.

glass-house.q: What is different about the room behind the glass?
options: It looks the same, but things go the other way
glass-house.evidence: First, there’s the room you can see through the glass—that’s just the same as our drawing-room, only the things go the other way.
glass-house.hint: Look again at what Alice tells Kitty about Looking-glass House.

live-flowers.q: When Alice wanted to reach the Red Queen, what did the Rose advise?
options: To run as fast as she could
To wait for the Queen to come to her
live-flowers.evidence: “You can’t possibly do that,” said the Rose: “I should advise you to walk the other way.”
live-flowers.hint: Look again at what the flowers tell Alice.

live-flowers.q: Why did Alice and the Red Queen run so fast but stay in the same place?
options: In Looking-glass land it takes all the running you can do to stay where you are
They were running on a moving road
They were running in circles on purpose
live-flowers.evidence: “Now, here, you see, it takes all the running you can do, to keep in the same place.
live-flowers.hint: Look again at what the Red Queen says when they stop running.

live-flowers.q: Why is Alice’s journey across the country like a game of chess?
options: She moves square by square like a pawn, to become a Queen
She has to beat the Red Queen at chess
The flowers are all chess pieces
live-flowers.evidence: You can be the White Queen’s Pawn, if you like, as Lily’s too young to play; and you’re in the Second Square to begin with: when you get to the Eighth Square you’ll be a Queen—”
live-flowers.hint: Look again at what the Red Queen offers Alice.

insects.q: What did the guard on the train ask everyone for?
insects.evidence: “Tickets, please!” said the guard, putting his head in at the window.
insects.hint: Look again at the start of the train ride.

insects.q: Why did the Fawn walk happily with Alice through the wood?
options: In that wood, nobody could remember names — so it didn’t know she was a human child
Alice gave it something to eat
It was lost and needed help
insects.evidence: “I’m a Fawn!” it cried out in a voice of delight, “and, dear me! you’re a human child!”
insects.hint: Look again at what happens when they come out of the wood.

insects.q: What is strange about the wood Alice walks into?
insects.evidence: “This must be the wood,” she said thoughtfully to herself, “where things have no names.
insects.hint: Look again at what the Gnat tells Alice about the wood.

tweedles.q: In the rhyme, what did Tweedledum and Tweedledee agree to have?
tweedles.hint: Look again at the rhyme Alice remembers about them.

tweedles.q: In the rhyme, why did Tweedledum want to fight?
options: He said Tweedledee had spoiled his nice new rattle
They both wanted the same hat

tweedles.q: Tweedledee tells Alice she is only a thing in the Red King’s dream. What does Alice ask back?
options: If she’s only in his dream, then what are they?
Can she wake the King up?
What is the King dreaming about?
tweedles.evidence: “Besides, if I’m only a sort of thing in his dream, what are you, I should like to know?”
tweedles.hint: Look again at the part where they find the Red King snoring.

wool-water.q: What is the White Queen’s rule about jam?
options: Jam tomorrow and jam yesterday — but never jam today
wool-water.evidence: “The rule is, jam tomorrow and jam yesterday—but never jam today.”
wool-water.hint: Look again at what the White Queen offers Alice as wages.

wool-water.q: Why does Alice suddenly find herself rowing a boat?
options: The Sheep pushed her into the stream
wool-water.evidence: Alice was beginning to say, when suddenly the needles turned into oars in her hands, and she found they were in a little boat, gliding along between banks
wool-water.hint: Look again at the part in the Sheep’s shop.

wool-water.q: Why can Alice never have “jam today”?
options: It’s jam every OTHER day, and today is never “another” day
The jam has all been eaten
wool-water.evidence: “It’s jam every other day: today isn’t any other day, you know.”
wool-water.hint: Look again at how the White Queen explains her rule.

options: On top of a high, narrow wall
humpty.evidence: on the top of a high wall—such a narrow one that Alice quite wondered how he could keep his balance
humpty.hint: Look again at how Alice first sees him.

humpty.q: Why did Humpty Dumpty get a present when it wasn’t his birthday?
options: He found it on the wall
humpty.evidence: Humpty Dumpty continued thoughtfully, as he crossed one knee over the other and clasped his hands round it, “they gave it me—for an un-birthday present.”
humpty.hint: Look again at what Humpty says about his cravat.

humpty.q: Humpty says the question is “which is to be master”. What does he mean?
options: Whether he controls what words mean, or the words control him
Who is the master of the wall
Whether Alice or he is cleverer
humpty.evidence: “The question is,” said Humpty Dumpty, “which is to be master—that’s all.”
humpty.hint: Look again at the argument about the word “glory”.

lion-unicorn.q: What were the Lion and the Unicorn fighting for?
lion-unicorn.hint: Look again at what the White King tells Alice.

lion-unicorn.q: Why does the King call it “the best of the joke”?
options: It’s his own crown they’re fighting for
lion-unicorn.evidence: “Yes, to be sure,” said the King: “and the best of the joke is, that it’s my crown all the while!
lion-unicorn.hint: Look again at what the King says about the crown.

lion-unicorn.q: How do you serve Looking-glass cake?
options: Hand it round first, and cut it afterwards
Cut it first, then hand it round
lion-unicorn.evidence: “Hand it round first, and cut it afterwards.”
lion-unicorn.hint: Look again at the part where Alice tries to cut the cake.

white-knight.q: Who rescued Alice from the Red Knight?
white-knight.evidence: “Yes, but then I came and rescued her!” the White Knight replied.
white-knight.hint: Look again at the start of the chapter.

white-knight.q: Why does the White Knight carry his little box upside-down?
options: So the rain can’t get in
white-knight.evidence: You see I carry it upside-down, so that the rain can’t get in.”
white-knight.hint: Look again at the part about the deal box on his shoulder.

white-knight.q: Alice says he hasn’t had much practice in riding. Why does she think so?
options: He keeps tumbling off his horse
white-knight.evidence: “I’m afraid you’ve not had much practice in riding,” she ventured to say, as she was helping him up from his fifth tumble.
white-knight.hint: Look again at how many times he falls off.

queen-alice.q: What words were over the doorway Alice came to?
queen-alice.evidence: She was standing before an arched doorway over which were the words Queen Alice in large letters
queen-alice.hint: Look again at the arched doorway.

queen-alice.q: Why did the leg of mutton bow to Alice?
queen-alice.evidence: “You look a little shy; let me introduce you to that leg of mutton,” said the Red Queen.

queen-alice.q: Alice is afraid her crown might come off, but says she’ll manage it “in time”. What does that show?
options: She is getting used to being a Queen
She doesn’t want to be a Queen
The crown is much too big
queen-alice.evidence: “and if I really am a Queen,” she said as she sat down again, “I shall be able to manage it quite well in time.”
queen-alice.hint: Look again at the part when Alice first finds the crown.

vault.q: How did Alice become a Queen?
options: She moved across the board like a pawn, to the Eighth Square
The White King gave her a crown
vault.evidence: when you get to the Eighth Square you’ll be a Queen—”
vault.hint: Think about what the Red Queen told her at the start.

vault.q: In Looking-glass land, what do you have to do to stay in the same place?
options: Run as fast as you can
vault.evidence: “Now, here, you see, it takes all the running you can do, to keep in the same place.
vault.hint: Think about the run with the Red Queen.

vault.q: Which rule about jam does the White Queen have?
options: Jam tomorrow and jam yesterday, but never jam today
vault.evidence: “The rule is, jam tomorrow and jam yesterday—but never jam today.”

vault.q: What did the Red Queen turn out to be when Alice shook her?
options: A chess piece made of wood
vault.evidence: —and it really was a kitten, after all.

vault.q: What does Alice say about the Red King at the end?
options: He was part of her dream — but she was part of his dream too
He was the one who woke her up
He was never in the story
vault.evidence: He was part of my dream, of course—but then I was part of his dream, too!
vault.hint: Think about the last chapter, “Which Dreamed It?”

vault.q: Who did Alice talk to about her adventure when she woke up?
vault.evidence: And you’ve been along with me, Kitty—all through the Looking-Glass world.
vault.hint: Think about the very last pages.
